prompt: What does a split into specialists change, according to the lesson?

choices.text: How expert each agent is, since a specialist's model is tuned to its domain
choices.why: The specialists call the same model as everyone else. Nothing makes them more expert.

choices.text: What each agent sees and what each is allowed to do
choices.why: Right. Context, tools and privileges per agent are the real levers.

choices.text: The price per token, which providers discount for multi-agent systems
choices.why: Price per token does not depend on how the program arranges its calls.

choices.text: Nothing but the organisation chart
choices.why: It changes context, tools and privileges, and those are real.

prompt: Which of these are real reasons to split work across agents? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A shorter conversation per agent
choices.why: Yes. Each specialist starts from one question, not the whole history.

choices.text: Fewer tools for each model to choose between
choices.why: Yes. Choosing between two tools goes wrong less than choosing between twenty.

choices.text: An agent that reads untrusted text having no tools that act
choices.why: Yes. Least privilege per agent, which lesson 17 builds on.

choices.text: Fewer requests per answer
choices.why: No. The split sent six requests where one agent sent two.

prompt: In a handoff, who answers the customer?

choices.text: The triage agent, after reading the specialist's answer
choices.why: Triage is out of the loop once it transfers. Nothing comes back to it.

choices.text: The orchestrator, which composes the specialists' answers
choices.why: That is the agents-as-tools shape.

choices.text: The specialist
choices.why: Right. It receives the conversation and answers it itself.

choices.text: A person
choices.why: A person may be a handoff target, but in this lesson the specialist answers.

prompt: Why does `transfer_to_orders` take no arguments while `ask_orders` takes a question?

choices.text: A transfer moves the whole conversation; the other expects a reply
choices.why: Right. In a handoff what moves is control and the conversation, so there is nothing to write.

choices.text: Because tools with no arguments are cheaper to call
choices.why: Cost is not the reason; the shapes do different things.

choices.text: Because the triage agent cannot write text, only choose a tool name
choices.why: It could write text; the transfer has nothing to say beyond its name.

choices.text: Because labllm does not support arguments
choices.why: Every other tool in the lesson takes arguments through labllm.

prompt: Match each SDK feature to the shape it implements.
right_distractors: A single agent with every tool

prompt: What did the orders specialist know about the customer's message?

choices.text: All of it, since every agent in multi.py shares one conversation
choices.why: Each loop has its own messages. The specialist started from one question.

choices.text: Only the question the orchestrator wrote
choices.why: Right. 'Has order M-1043 shipped?' is its whole knowledge of the conversation.

choices.text: The customer's message and the catalogue specialist's answer
choices.why: The specialists never see each other's work.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: It knew the question it was asked, which is why it could answer.

prompt: Both specialists were asked in the orchestrator's first reply. What does that resemble from lesson 4?

choices.text: The validation gate that refused bad arguments
choices.why: Nothing was refused here.

choices.text: The idempotency key on refunds
choices.why: No write happened in this run.

choices.text: The error result for a missing order
choices.why: Both lookups succeeded.

choices.text: Two tool calls in one reply
choices.why: Right. To the orchestrator, each specialist is a tool, and independent calls go together.

prompt: How many requests did the orchestrated run send in total, across all three agents?
How many more input tokens did the orchestrated run use than the single agent, for the same answer?
When does the lesson say the split's arithmetic turns in its favour?

choices.text: Whenever the question has two or more parts to answer
choices.why: This lesson's question had two parts and the split was pure overhead.

choices.text: When the specialists use cheaper models than the orchestrator
choices.why: A possible saving, but not the argument made in the lesson.

choices.text: When long sub-tasks would otherwise fill one conversation that every later request resends
choices.why: Right. Ten steps of research inside one agent are paid for again in every later request; inside a specialist, only there.

choices.text: Never
choices.why: The lesson names three cases where it pays.

prompt: The triage agent's only request produced one output token. Why so few?

choices.text: Because the decision is the tool's name, and its input is empty
choices.why: Right. transfer_to_orders takes no arguments, so the reply is a name and {}.

choices.text: Because max_tokens was set to one
choices.why: max_tokens was 200.

choices.text: Because the triage agent failed and the host retried it with a smaller limit
choices.why: Nothing failed; the transfer happened on the first request.

choices.text: Because labllm counts tool names as zero tokens
choices.why: The output count covers the tool input; the decision itself is cheap.

prompt: After the handoff, the customer's next message asks about books. What goes wrong, and what fixes it?

choices.text: Nothing: the orders specialist can answer anything about the shop
choices.why: It has get_order and search_help, and no catalogue tool.

choices.text: The triage agent answers instead, since it saw the first message
choices.why: Triage is out of the loop after a handoff unless the design brings it back.

choices.text: The customer has to open a new conversation for books
choices.why: That pushes a design gap onto the customer.

choices.text: The specialist has no catalogue tool; give specialists a way back to triage
choices.why: Right. A transfer_to_triage tool, or routing each new message through triage again.

prompt: An orchestrator asks a specialist 'Check the customer's order'. What is wrong with that question?

choices.text: It is too short for the provider to accept as a tool argument
choices.why: Short arguments are fine; the problem is what is missing.

choices.text: It omits the id, and the specialist has nobody to ask
choices.why: Right. A question has to carry its own context: ids, constraints, what was tried.

choices.text: It should be written in the customer's own words
choices.why: The customer's words may not contain the id either; self-contained is the rule.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: The specialist starts from that sentence alone.

prompt: Why does the lesson apply data minimisation at every boundary between agents?

choices.text: Because providers refuse requests with personal data
choices.why: They do not refuse it; the point is not sending more than the job needs.

choices.text: Because tokens are cheaper when the text contains no names
choices.why: Token cost does not depend on whether text is personal.

choices.text: Each boundary hands the data to one more agent
choices.why: Right. A specialist that needs an order id should not also get the customer's address.

choices.text: Because agents cannot read personal data
choices.why: They can, which is exactly why it should not reach them needlessly.

prompt: Without --evidence, why did the orchestrator tell the customer both orders were on their way?

choices.text: Because get_order returned the wrong status for M-1048
choices.why: It returned cancelled, correctly. The specialist's summary dropped it.

choices.text: It saw only the summary, and the summary hid the cancellation
choices.why: Right. Nothing else crossed the boundary, so it had no way to tell.

choices.text: Because the orchestrator called get_order itself and misread the result
choices.why: The orchestrator has no shop tools; it only asks specialists.

choices.text: Because the specialist lied
choices.why: Its sentence is defensible word by word; it lost a fact, it did not invent one.

prompt: Why does the host, rather than the specialist, attach the evidence?

choices.text: Because the host attaches it for every call, so the specialist cannot leave anything out
choices.why: Right. Asking the specialist to include its evidence would be one more thing for it to summarise away.

choices.text: Because specialists are not allowed to write more than two sentences
choices.why: That limit is in the prompt, and the reason is completeness, not length.

choices.text: Because evidence costs no tokens when the host adds it
choices.why: It costs tokens either way; the lesson says so.

choices.text: For speed
choices.why: Speed is not the point; completeness is.

prompt: With --evidence, what changed in the specialist's behaviour?

choices.text: It wrote a more careful summary that mentioned the cancelled order
choices.why: Its sentence was word for word the same, as the last command printed.

choices.text: It made two extra tool calls to double-check the statuses
choices.why: It made the same two calls as before.

choices.text: It refused to answer without evidence
choices.why: It answered exactly as before.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The specialist did not improve; the boundary did.

prompt: Which question, on its own, settles that two agents should be split?

choices.text: Whether the question has more than one part
choices.why: Two parts were pure overhead in this lesson.

choices.text: One reads untrusted text, the other acts
choices.why: Right. Splitting the reader from the actor is a security design, and it stands on its own.

choices.text: Whether the team already has an org chart with matching departments
choices.why: Organisation charts are not evidence about the task.

choices.text: Whether the model supports tools
choices.why: Every agent here needs tools, split or not.

prompt: Put the orchestrated run of section 04 in order.
items: The orchestrator asks both specialists in one reply
Each specialist runs its own tool call
Each specialist's answer returns as a tool result
The orchestrator writes the reply to the customer

prompt: In the handoff run, the triage agent called `transfer_to____`.
Which design does the lesson say most production agents are?

choices.text: An orchestrator with a specialist for every department of the business
choices.why: Most are not; those that are got there by measuring a single agent first.

choices.text: A chain of handoffs from triage to a specialist and on to a reviewer
choices.why: Possible, but not what the lesson says is most common.

choices.text: One loop with a handful of good tools
choices.why: Right. Effort goes into tools, limits and tests before anything is split.

choices.text: A group of agents that vote
choices.why: Voting is a parallelisation pattern, not the common production design.
